newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian weather-Mixed blessings for sugar, rice.
newsitem.headline: Australian weather-Mixed blessings for sugar, rice.

text.p: Australian crops are receiving mixed effects from the El Nino weather pattern, with Queensland sugar hampered perversely by rain, the coming rice crop being set up well by dry conditions, and wheat continuing to survive once-threatened devastation.

Wheat, the most important crop in terms of value, remains in reasonable shape after last week's good rainfall of up to 50 mm across almost all of the southern half of Australia, analysts said. Only scattered showers fell over the weekend.

But onshore coastal showers over the past couple of weeks, a result of a high pressure front in the south, has been causing Australia's sugarcane crop problems in Queensland's far north, Ross Chapman, deputy general manager of grower organisation CANEGROWERS told Reuters.
This had slowed cane harvesting and made conditions very difficult, he said.
"We're certainly having problems up north. The sugar content of the cane is lower than it should be as well," he said.
It was too early to say how this would affect cane and sugar production, but it had delayed the harvest, he said.

Queensland Sugar Corp (QSC), owner of almost all of Australia's annual sugar production, sees the cane crop in Australia's main competitor, Thailand, as hit far more adversely by dry conditions associated with the El Nino weather effect.

With Thailand's anticipated 1997/98 sugarcane production scaled back to less than 50 million tonnes from 56 million tonnes the year before, the rise in U.S. sugar futures on Friday was not driven by Queensland, a QSC official said.
The sugar market was being supported by 1997/98 appearing likely to show a world sugar deficit for the first time in three years, he said.
The sugar market would also react to the weather, he said.

The weather was so far looking good for Australia's rice-growing areas, in the Murray River area in the New South Wales-Victoria border region, as farmers prepared to plant at the end of September, Chris Black, spokesman for the Ricegrowers Cooperative Ltd, told Reuters.
"This dry weather allows them to do that with a level of orderly management, rather than ducking in between storm clouds," he said.
"Good rains and snowfalls in the mountain catchment areas were 'something of a godsend'", he said.
"It is looking good and if we have dry ... weather from October through until March next year, sunshine is what we crave," he said.
Ricegrowing areas had this season had exactly that, he said.

Black also noted that state governments, which control water supplies, have promised that the crop will not be disrupted by current controversies over the New South Wales government's water reform process.
The Australian industry expected to produce about 1.2 million tonnes of rice in its next crop, against the record 1.38 million tonnes in 1996/97, Black said.
This in turn was up from the slightly more than 950,000 tonnes produced the year before in growing conditions affected by cool weather.

Broker Phil Lindsay of Ord Minnett Jardine Fleming Futures said markets in agricultural commodities in Southeast Asia, including Australia -- sugar, wheat, canola, rice and cotton -- all now had an in-built El Nino factor.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
